title: Donald "DJ" Johnson - Wikipedia
notes: Donald Johnson Jr., also Beanz; born 13 March 1983 in Houston; drums, keyboards, bass, vocals; active from 2004. Grew up playing drums, moved to the organ in his late teens; Texas All State Symphonic Wind Ensemble; orchestral percussion with Jim Whitfill. Met Mark Speer in 2004 (at the Red Cat Jazz Cafe); both hired players in Pastor Rudy Rasmus's gospel band at St. John's United Methodist, Johnson on organ. Half of the hip-hop production duo Beanz N Kornbread (with Kenneth Roy). Plays a jazz kit, smaller than many rock drummers'; "He is left-handed"; typically does not record to a click track. Quotes Modern Drummer (2020) for his kit.

title: Khruangbin - Wikipedia
notes: Houston trio: Laura Lee (Ochoa), bass; Mark Speer, guitar; Donald "DJ" Johnson, drums. Speer and Johnson met in 2004 in Rudy Rasmus's gospel band at St. John's, Johnson on organ; after Lee and Speer toured with Yppah in 2010, they asked Johnson to join "to play simple break-beats" under the guitar and bass. Their early sound made in a barn in Burton, Texas; a long working relationship with the Houston engineer Steve Christensen. Albums: The Universe Smiles Upon You (6 November 2015, Night Time Stories), Con Todo el Mundo (26 January 2018), Mordechai (26 June 2020), Ali with Vieux Farka Touré (2022), A La Sala (2024), The Universe Smiles Upon You ii (2025); EPs with Leon Bridges, Texas Sun (2020) and Texas Moon (2022).

title: The Universe Smiles Upon You - Wikipedia
notes: Released 6 November 2015 on Night Time Stories. Personnel: Laura Lee, bass and vocals; Mark Speer, guitar, percussion and vocals; Donald "DJ" Johnson, drums; Wilhelm Van Horn, pedal steel.

title: Khruangbin's DJ Johnson (Modern Drummer, Ilya Stemkovsky, 2020)
notes: Read from the Wayback Machine copy of 25 July 2020. "Donald Ray 'DJ' Johnson", thirty-six, from the Texas church tradition; Texas All-State Jazz Ensembles; orchestral percussion with Jim Whitfield. "I was never a chops-oriented drummer. I focused on drum breaks or breakbeats. I would mimic those as closely as possible, down to the tone of the drum or the opening or tone of the hi-hat ... I studied the nuances of a groove as opposed to its surface ... I learned how to mix myself on the kit." Influences: Clyde Stubblefield and Jabo Starks, Bernard Purdie, James Gadson, Ed Greene's Barry White cuts, JR Robinson, Al Jackson, Ernie Isley, Buddy Miles, Sade's drummers Dave Early and Martin Ditcham, Jeff Porcaro, Earl Palmer on David Axelrod's records, Carlton Barrett and Style Scott. From church: "it's not about you; you disappear". The band records the foundations together and plays its parts together for the first time. Live they play the sources of hip-hop samples, Porcaro's part on "I Keep Forgettin'" with the keyboard in his left hand. "I use a leather strip on the head, which drops the drum in pitch. So it allows me to play a piccolo snare everywhere I go. The leather doesn't cover the entire head, just a portion of it, including the center." "We never use a click on anything." Kit: a 3x13 Diamond Drum Co. maple snare, a 14x14 Gretsch floor tom, a 14x20 Gretsch bass drum; 14" CB Percussion MX hats, an 18" Meinl Byzance Dark crash; Promark DJ Johnson signature sticks; a Yamaha reface keyboard, played left-handed.

title: Leon Bridges & Khruangbin's DJ Johnson Talk Magic Of New EP 'Texas Moon' (GRAMMY.com, Ana Monroy Yglesias, 22 February 2022)
notes: Johnson started on drums at two or three, after his uncle, the drummer John Foster; quit the drums later "because there's so many dope drummers in Houston"; Speer's asking him was "my red carpet back to the drum set". The EPs recorded with Steve Christensen, Bridges playing guitar and singing; "for us, they were like concerts". He played piano on Conversion; the slow, spacious feel owes to Houston's chopped and screwed.

title: Khruangbin interview (Live For Live Music, Andrew O'Brien, 21 August 2019)
notes: DJ "sticks to simple breakbeats on a simple kit, staying dutifully in the cut with nary a drum fill to be found." On fills: "Depends on your definition of 'drum fill.'" "No drum solos." "Keep it simple. Because the music just doesn't need it ... The music tells you what it needs."
